newsitem.title: USA: U.S. foreign aid wins tentative approval.
newsitem.headline: U.S. foreign aid wins tentative approval.

text.p: A U.S. House of Representatives-Senate conference reached tentative agreement on Tuesday to provide $12.1 billion in foreign aid next year, but failed to resolve an abortion-related dispute over international family planning aid.

The international family planning aid dispute and the White House objections to cuts in the bill make it likely the final 1997 foreign aid package will be wrapped into a broad government spending bill to be negotiated between the White House and Congress.
As approved by the House, international family planning agencies would receive full U.S. funding only if they pledged not to perform abortions.
While they now are not permitted to use U.S. funds to pay for abortion services, they would also have to pledge not to use privately raised money for abortions.
The Senate did not include this restriction in its version of the 1997 foreign aid bill and the White House has said the provision makes the bill a strong candidate for a veto.

As proposed, the compromise bill would supply about $800 million less in aid to international agencies and other countries than sought by President Bill Clinton. It is essentially the same level supplied by Congress last year when foreign aid was cut by $1.5 billion.
Again, the bulk of the money will go to fulfil commitments to the Middle East, with $3.1 billion in military and economic aid allocated to Israel and $2 billion of both for Egypt.
Over the White House objections, the Agency for International Development was cut by $30 million from 1996 levels and will receive $135 million less than Clinton sought.
The conference refused to revive funding for the African Development Bank at the $66 million level requested by the administration. Congress terminated funding last year.
The International Development Administration was allotted $700 million, equal to the 1996 level but $234 million below the president's budget.
The House and Senate negotiators also agreed to fund the Overseas Private Investment Corporation and to keep the 1996 level of $19.6 million in funding for Ireland.
